chunks: 31 - What Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Qattān told us, he said: Ahmad ibn Yahyā ibn Zakariyyā al-Qattān told us, from Bakr ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ḥabīb, he said: Tamīm ibn Bahlūl told us, from his father, from Sulaymān ibn Ḥafṣ al-Marwazī, from Sulaymān ibn Mihrān, he said: I said to Ja‘far ibn Muḥammad (peace be upon them):

“Is it permissible for us to say: Indeed, Allāh, the Mighty and Exalted, is in a place?” He said: “Glory be to Allāh and Exalted is He from that! Indeed, if He were in a place, He would be created (muḥdath), because that which exists in a place is in need of the place, and need (iḥtiyāj) is from the attributes of the created (muḥdath), not from the attributes of the Eternal (al-Qadīm).”

key_terms.الْقَدِيم: The Eternal (that which has no beginning)
key_terms.مُحْدَث: Created / Caused (that which has a beginning)

ai.seo_question: Why is God not considered to be in a place according to Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this foundational hadith from al-Ṣadūq’s *al-Tawḥīd*, Imām Ja‘far al-Ṣādiq (AS) employs the logical attribute of 'neediness' (iḥtiyāj) to refute spatial containment, arguing that anything located in a place is dependent upon it and thus created (muḥdath). This reasoning establishes that Allah’s transcendence (tanzīh) precludes Him from being bounded by space, time, or direction, a core tenet of Shia theological ontology. The narration underscores that divine essence is not a body or entity occupying a locus, but rather the Necessary Existent whose attributes are identical to His essence.
